title: Seventy Years and the Cup of Wrath
summary: In 605 BC, the year Nebuchadnezzar came to power, Jeremiah looks back on twenty-three years of preaching that Judah refused to hear and announces that the LORD will bring Babylon against the land, which will serve the king of Babylon for seventy years before Babylon itself is judged. Then he is given a cup of the wine of God's wrath to make the nations drink, beginning with Jerusalem and ending with Babylon. The chapter closes with the LORD roaring like a lion over the whole earth and its shepherds wailing.
story: This chapter is a hinge in the book. Chapters 1 to 24 have been largely Jeremiah's warnings to Judah; here those warnings are summed up and given a date, and the horizon widens from Judah to every nation. The seventy years set a limit on Babylon's power and so contain the first glimmer of hope, which chapter 29 will develop for the exiles. The cup passage previews the oracles against the nations in chapters 46 to 51, which end with Babylon's fall. From here on the book alternates between stories of Jeremiah's conflict with kings and prophets (26 to 29, 32 to 45) and the promises of restoration (30 to 33).
historical:
Verse 1 synchronizes two reigns: the fourth year of Jehoiakim was the first year of Nebuchadnezzar. That is 605 BC, the year Nebuchadnezzar, as crown prince, crushed the Egyptian army at Carchemish on the Euphrates (46:2 dates that battle to the same year) and then became king on his father Nabopolassar's death. Carchemish settled that Babylon, not Egypt, would dominate the lands along the eastern Mediterranean. Jeremiah's twenty-three years run back to the thirteenth year of Josiah, about 627 BC, when his call came (1:2).

The seventy years (verses 11-12, and again in 29:10) have been counted in several ways. Babylon fell to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BC, roughly seventy years after its rise to dominance around 609 to 605 BC. Others count from the temple's destruction in 587 or 586 BC to its rebuilding, finished around 516 BC, which is how Zechariah 1:12 and 7:5 appear to reckon it. Many scholars also see seventy as a round number for a full lifetime (Psalm 90:10), long enough that the generation taken into exile would mostly die there; Isaiah 23:15 uses the same span for Tyre. Later biblical writers returned to Jeremiah's number: 2 Chronicles 36:21 connects it to the land's unpaid Sabbath rests, Ezra 1:1 sees Cyrus's decree as its fulfillment, and Daniel 9:2 shows Daniel studying it.
cultural:
Verse 10 lists the sounds of an ordinary town: wedding songs, the grinding of millstones each morning as women made the day's flour, and oil lamps burning in houses at night. Their disappearance is a picture of total desolation, a place where no one marries, eats, or lives. The cup in verses 15 to 29 draws on a familiar image. In Israel's poetry God's judgment is a cup the guilty must drink until they stagger (Psalm 75:8; Isaiah 51:17), and a cup forced on a guest was a sign of humiliation.

The list of nations in verses 18 to 26 maps the world as Judah knew it, running from Egypt through the Philistine cities, the neighboring kingdoms of Edom, Moab, and Ammon, the Phoenician ports of Tyre and Sidon, the Arabian oases of Dedan and Tema, and east to Elam and Media. “Sheshach” in verse 26 is a code name for Babylon made by a Hebrew letter substitution (known later as atbash) that swaps the first letter of the alphabet with the last, the second with the second-to-last, and so on; the same device appears in 51:41. The location of Zimri (verse 25) is unknown.
literary: The chapter has two main parts. Verses 1 to 14 are a prose sermon that summarizes Jeremiah's message to date, with the refrain “you have not listened” and the key word “seventy.” Verses 15 to 38 are a symbolic action (the cup) followed by poetic oracles of worldwide judgment. The roaring lion of verses 30 and 38 frames the poetry, and the shepherds of verses 34 to 36 are the rulers of the nations, echoing Jeremiah's condemnation of Judah's shepherds in chapter 23. Verse 13 refers to “all that is written in this book.” In the Greek translation of Jeremiah (the Septuagint, made by Jews in the centuries before Christ), which is about one-eighth shorter than the Hebrew, the oracles against the nations are placed right after this verse rather than at chapters 46 to 51. Scholars debate which arrangement is older.

outline.t: Babylon as God's instrument; seventy years, then Babylon's judgment
The cup of the wine of wrath passed to the nations
The LORD roars against the earth; the shepherds wail

doctrines.note: God calls Nebuchadnezzar “My servant” (verse 9) without making him righteous. The empire serves God's purpose unknowingly and is then held accountable for its own guilt (verse 12). The LORD rules the nations and sets limits to their power.
Judgment begins with the city that bears God's name (verse 29) and then extends to all the earth. Being God's people is no exemption; it is the reason judgment starts there.
Verses 3 to 7 show God's patience: prophet after prophet, again and again, calling people to turn from evil ways. Judgment comes only after a long refusal.

words.note: Shiv'im, seventy. Seven was a number of completeness in Israel, and seventy (seven times ten) suggests a full, fixed span. Whether counted exactly or as a round figure, the number assures the exiles that Babylon's rule has an end date set by God.
Kos, cup. It can be a cup of blessing or salvation (Psalm 23:5; 116:13), but in the prophets it often holds God's wrath. Jeremiah's cup must be drunk by every nation, including Judah.
Eved, servant or slave. Used in verse 4 of the prophets, God's faithful servants, and in verse 9 of Nebuchadnezzar. The word describes a role in God's plan, not moral approval.
Sha'ag, to roar, the sound of a lion over its prey. Amos opens his book with the same picture of the LORD roaring from Zion (Amos 1:2). Here the roar goes out over all the earth.

christ: The cup of wrath is one of the images the New Testament uses to explain the cross. In Gethsemane Jesus prays that the Father would take this cup from him, yet not what he wills but what the Father wills (Mark 14:36). Christians have long read that prayer against passages like this one: the cup the nations deserved to drink, Jesus chose to drink. That connection is drawn from the shared prophetic image rather than from a direct citation of this chapter, and it should be held with that care. Revelation, on the other hand, does echo this chapter directly. Its lament over fallen Babylon says that the sound of the millstone, the light of a lamp, and the voice of bride and bridegroom will never be heard there again (Revelation 18:22-23), turning Jeremiah's words against Judah into a verdict on the final Babylon, the proud power that opposes God.

hard.q: Did the seventy years actually add up, and how should we read the number?
hard.a: Believing readers have answered in more than one way. Some take the number as precise and look for a seventy-year span: from Babylon's rise in 609 to 605 BC to its fall in 539 BC, or from the temple's destruction in 587 or 586 BC to its rebuilding around 516 BC. Both work closely, and the Bible itself seems to use both reckonings (Ezra 1:1 ties it to Cyrus; Zechariah 1:12 ties it to the ruined temple). Others read seventy as a round number for a lifetime, the ordinary span of human years in Psalm 90:10, meaning that the exile would last long enough to outlast the generation that caused it. Either way, what matters is the limit. The prophecy tells the exiles not to expect a quick return (the false prophets of chapter 28 promised two years) and not to despair of any return at all. It also shows how later Scripture wrestled with the number: Daniel 9 reads Jeremiah's seventy years and receives a vision of seventy weeks of years, reapplying the prophecy to a longer horizon.

questions: Jeremiah preached for twenty-three years without being heeded. What sustains someone who keeps speaking the truth when no one seems to listen?
God calls a pagan emperor his servant. How does that change the way you think about powers and rulers in your own time?
Judgment begins with the city that bears God's name. What would it mean for the church to take that seriously rather than assuming it is exempt?
